A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ST-WebAgentBench and provide readable main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices. Content can be matched across the expanded benchmark and appendix renumbering; no material reading gaps prevent comparison.

before.justification: v5 reports original evaluations of three web agents, policy-dimension ablations, policy-load analyses, and an expert-panel study.

after.justification: v6 retains these original empirical results and additionally reports all-pass@3 outcomes for the three evaluated agents.

M1.justification: The policy hierarchy, POLICY_CONTEXT injection, template evaluators, and simulated user-confirmation mechanism are retained. RapidFuzz is newly specified for existing fuzzy matching, without establishing an algorithm replacement. The controller architecture remains future work in v5 Appendix H and v6 Appendix I.

E1.justification: The three applications remain, but v6 adds 80 SuiteCRM Modality Challenge tasks, divided into 40 Vision-Advantage and 40 DOM-Advantage tasks. Color, layout, chart, offscreen-content, and hidden-metadata scenarios introduce distinct perceptual requirements beyond simply increasing task counts (Section 3.5; Appendix H.4).

E2.justification: Both versions evaluate AWM, WorkArena-Legacy, and WebVoyager. No additional comparator participates in the reported agent comparisons. Historical leaderboard model-label edits in Table 4 and additional related-work citations do not establish changes to the evaluated comparator set.

E3.justification: v5 explicitly reports single pass@1 evaluation; v6 reports pass@3 and adds all-pass@k. Table 2 changes the suite from 222 tasks and 646 policies to 375 tasks and 3,057 policies, substantially revises application composition, and introduces difficulty subsets and modality controls. These are reported protocol changes; the PDFs do not establish how retained results were rerun.

E4.justification: v6 adds a repeated-run reliability analysis through all-pass@3, probing whether success persists across attempts. The dimension-removal ablation in Table 3 and policy-load analysis in Appendix C remain. The new modality illustrations explain diagnostic scenarios but provide no separate modality-ablation performance results.

E5.justification: The stated run count changes from one to three, and all-pass@3 adds reporting of consistency across runs. Existing significance and slope-uncertainty reporting in Appendix C is unchanged; no seeds or new confidence intervals are supplied. The retained 'executed once per agent' wording leaves the execution accounting unclear.

E6.justification: Figure 2 adds all-pass@3 scores of 5.0% for AWM, 2.0% for WebVoyager, and 3.0% for WorkArena. Existing completion metrics, risk plots, Table 3 correlations, and Appendix C trends retain their numerical values. Because the reported suite and run protocol change, these retained numbers do not establish same-setting performance stability.

T1.justification: Section 3.3 adds a mathematical definition of all-pass@k as the fraction of tasks completed in every run, including all-pass@1 = CR. The existing policy action-set restriction and CR, CuP, PCR, pCuP, and Risk Ratio definitions remain unchanged; no new proofs are introduced.

C1.justification: The central claim that task completion masks policy violations remains. v6 adds abstract claims about difficulty profiling and modality isolation, and conclusion-level controller design principles. The introduction softens 'first benchmark' and 'first principled standard' positioning toward a 'first step' and 'a principled standard.'

C2.justification: v6 adds an explicit threat model and excluded attack classes (Appendix G.1), limitations concerning the shared GPT-4o backbone and omitted proprietary agents, and explanations involving overgeneralization and loss of policy awareness. Appendix I newly asserts that continuous policy injection reduces drift relative to initialization-only hints, although no corresponding controlled comparison is reported.

D1.justification: v6 newly identifies the common GPT-4o backbone and deterministic RapidFuzz judging, updates repository structure and validation/generation utilities, and corrects JSON and code examples. Direct GitHub and Hugging Face links replace project-site links. Much of the existing prompt template, evaluator code, and environment documentation is retained.

R1.justification: v6 adds citations to IDA, SNAP, IBM generalist-agent deployment, and earlier process-automation work while retaining the main related-work argument. The publication update for From Grounding to Planning and the documented Multion/AGI renaming are matched as existing references, rather than treated as new research.

P1.justification: There are targeted rewrites of the abstract, conclusion, evaluator descriptions, and examples, plus author/header edits and new subsections. The full policy template becomes Appendix F, shifting later appendices. The main five-section narrative and substantial portions of the existing prose remain intact.

P2.justification: v6 adopts the ICLR layout and substantially reformats appendix JSON/code displays. Table 1 gains a modality column, Table 2 gains subset structure, and Figure 2 gains all-pass@3 bars with revised legend and axis scaling. Five modality illustrations are added; the existing architecture diagram is retained as Figure 17.

improvement.justification: Broader scenarios, explicit threat boundaries, and clearer evaluator/access documentation improve usefulness. However, the expanded suite and pass@3 protocol are not reconciled with retained headline results and 'once per agent' wording. The all-pass formula checks completion, whereas Section 4.2 describes policy-compliant completion; the modality-unsolvability claim also conflicts with Figure 15's scrolling solution. These unresolved validity and reproducibility issues prevent a reliable net quality judgment.
